characters.description: A young gentlewoman rescued after a shipwreck on the coast of Illyria. Believing her twin brother Sebastian drowned and needing protection in an unfamiliar country, she disguises herself as a young man called Cesario and seeks employment in Orsino's household.
characters.name: Viola

characters.description: A seaman who rescues Viola after the wreck. He explains the political and social situation in Illyria and agrees to help her assume a male disguise, keeping her identity secret while she enters Orsino's service.
characters.name: Sea Captain

characters.description: Olivia's uncle, a convivial and disorderly resident of her household. He stays up drinking, resents restraint, and encourages Sir Andrew's courtship partly because Andrew's money supports their entertainment.
characters.name: Sir Toby Belch

characters.description: Olivia's practical waiting-gentlewoman. She trades sharp remarks with Sir Toby, criticizes his disruptive habits, and is comfortable enough in the household to challenge both servants and their social superiors.
characters.name: Maria

characters.description: A wealthy but foolish knight staying with Sir Toby in hopes of marrying Olivia. Easily flattered and discouraged, he boasts of accomplishments he cannot convincingly demonstrate and supplies money for Sir Toby's revels.
characters.name: Sir Andrew Aguecheek

characters.description: A wealthy countess mourning her dead brother and refusing Orsino's courtship. She intends to withdraw from society for years, though the arrival of Orsino's unusually eloquent new messenger soon unsettles that resolve.
characters.name: Olivia

characters.description: Olivia's steward, a grave and self-important servant who disapproves of the late-night pleasures of Sir Toby and his companions. He values order and takes pride in his own dignity and judgment.
characters.name: Malvolio

characters.description: Olivia's licensed fool, a singer and quick verbal performer whose apparent nonsense often exposes the folly of people with higher status. He has been absent from the household and must talk his way back into Olivia's favor.
characters.name: Feste

characters.description: Viola's twin brother, who also survives the shipwreck but believes Viola has drowned. Grief-stricken yet determined to travel on through Illyria, he resembles his sister closely enough that her male disguise makes the two nearly indistinguishable to strangers.
characters.name: Sebastian

characters.description: A sea captain who rescues Sebastian and becomes devoted to him. Although he has dangerous enemies in Orsino's territory because of an earlier naval conflict, he is reluctant to let Sebastian face Illyria alone.
characters.name: Antonio

characters.description: A gentleman serving Olivia who resents Malvolio for interfering with the household's amusements. He joins Sir Toby and Sir Andrew in hiding nearby while Malvolio discovers Maria's forged letter.
characters.name: Fabian

recaps.ending: In the final gathering, Sebastian's appearance proves that he and Viola are separate people and resolves the many mistakes caused by their resemblance. The twins recognize each other and rejoice that both survived the shipwreck. Olivia accepts that she has married Sebastian rather than Cesario, while Orsino learns that Cesario is Viola and turns his affection toward her; Viola will resume her female clothing once it is recovered. Maria's forged letter is exposed as the cause of Malvolio's humiliation. Sir Toby has married Maria, but Malvolio leaves vowing retaliation against the household. Orsino orders that he be pursued and reconciled if possible. The play closes with two newly acknowledged couples, Olivia and Sebastian and Orsino and Viola, while Feste remains to sing about the persistence of ordinary hardship beyond the festivities.
recaps.in_short: After a shipwreck separates twins Viola and Sebastian, Viola disguises herself as a young man named Cesario and serves Duke Orsino, who sends her to court the mourning Countess Olivia. Viola falls for Orsino, while Olivia falls for Cesario. In Olivia's household, Maria, Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, Fabian, and Feste punish the pompous steward Malvolio with a forged letter that persuades him Olivia loves him. Sebastian, also alive, enters Illyria with the loyal Antonio. Because he looks like the disguised Viola, he is mistaken for Cesario, accepts Olivia's sudden proposal, and baffles people involved in Sir Andrew's challenge. The confusions converge when both twins appear together. Viola reveals her identity; Orsino recognizes his love for her, and Olivia remains happily married to Sebastian. The prank on Malvolio is confessed, and he departs angrily while the household celebrates the paired marriages.

recaps.text: Duke Orsino of Illyria longs for Countess Olivia, who has withdrawn from courtship while mourning her brother. On the coast, Viola survives a shipwreck but believes her twin brother Sebastian has died. With a sea captain's help, she adopts male clothing and the name Cesario so she can safely enter Orsino's service. Elsewhere, Olivia's uncle Sir Toby drinks and makes noise in her house with Sir Andrew Aguecheek, a rich, inept suitor whom he encourages to keep pursuing Olivia. Maria, Olivia's waiting-gentlewoman, warns them that their conduct is unwelcome. Viola quickly gains Orsino's confidence. He sends Cesario to present his love to Olivia, while Viola privately realizes that she has fallen in love with Orsino herself.

Cesario gains an audience with Olivia and speaks for Orsino with such force that Olivia becomes interested in the messenger instead of the master. She sends Malvolio after Cesario with a ring and pretends it was left behind. Viola understands that Olivia has fallen for her male disguise and sees the emerging triangle: she loves Orsino, Orsino loves Olivia, and Olivia loves Cesario. Meanwhile, Sebastian is revealed to have survived the wreck. He believes Viola dead and prepares to travel into Illyria. Antonio, the captain who rescued him, cares for him deeply and decides to follow despite having enemies in Orsino's territory.

Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, and Feste hold a loud late-night gathering until Malvolio rebukes them and threatens to report Maria. In response, Maria devises a punishment based on Malvolio's vanity: she will imitate Olivia's handwriting in a letter suggesting that Olivia secretly loves him and wants him to behave in a series of conspicuous ways. Orsino continues confiding in Cesario about love. Viola comes close to describing her own feelings but cannot reveal her identity. At Olivia's house, Malvolio finds the planted letter while Maria and the others watch from hiding. He convinces himself it is genuine and resolves to approach Olivia smiling, wearing yellow stockings crossed with garters, and treating the rest of the household with arrogance. The tricksters are delighted that he has followed their design.

Olivia declares her love directly to Cesario, but Viola can only reject her. Sir Andrew decides to leave because Olivia favors the page; Sir Toby keeps him present by persuading him to challenge Cesario. Antonio catches up with Sebastian and gives him money before they separate to explore the town. Malvolio then appears before Olivia in the bizarre clothing and manner prescribed by the forged letter. Because Olivia knows nothing of the trick, she thinks he is mentally unwell and leaves Sir Toby to supervise him. Maria and her companions intensify the deception by treating Malvolio as possessed. At the same time, Sir Toby and Fabian frighten both Sir Andrew and the equally unwilling Cesario with exaggerated accounts of the other's skill in combat, forcing them toward a duel neither wants.

Antonio mistakes Cesario for Sebastian and intervenes in the duel. When officers arrest him, he asks for the money he gave Sebastian, but Viola cannot understand him and has none. Antonio interprets this as betrayal. His references to Sebastian give Viola hope that her brother may be alive. Sebastian then arrives and is repeatedly mistaken for Cesario. Unlike Viola, he responds forcefully when Sir Andrew and Sir Toby attack him. Olivia intervenes, addresses him as Cesario, and urges him to come with her. Though astonished by her affection and by the strange familiarity of everyone around him, Sebastian accepts the good fortune and agrees to marry her. Malvolio has meanwhile been confined in darkness. Feste disguises his voice as a learned examiner to torment him, then promises to carry out a letter in which Malvolio asks Olivia for release.

Orsino visits Olivia with Cesario. Olivia treats Cesario as her husband, while Antonio identifies the page as Sebastian, producing accusations of betrayal on every side. Sir Andrew and Sir Toby enter wounded and blame Cesario for beating them. The appearance of the real Sebastian finally separates the two identities. Sebastian and Viola recognize one another as the twins lost in the wreck, and Viola explains her disguise. Olivia accepts Sebastian as the man she married. Orsino, seeing that Cesario is Viola and recalling her devotion, asks Viola to become his wife once she resumes her own identity. Feste delivers Malvolio's letter, and Malvolio is released. Fabian and Feste explain Maria's forged message; Fabian also reports that Sir Toby has married Maria. Malvolio leaves in anger, promising revenge, while Orsino calls for an effort to make peace and prepares for the two marriages.

characters.description: The head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, the Soviet officer who ran the agent that destroyed the Circus and who has been Smiley's opponent for twenty years. He is known to the British only by a work name, a photograph and a career reconstructed from fragments: ascetic, unbribable, and safe from the ordinary levers because he appears to want nothing for himself. Smiley met him once, years ago, in an Indian jail, tried to turn him and failed, and gave him a cigarette lighter belonging to his wife.
characters.name: Karla

characters.description: A Russian emigree living in modest circumstances in Paris, ageing, unwell and alone, who left the Soviet Union many years ago and had to leave a daughter behind. She is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who offers, on conditions, to have the girl allowed out to join her. Suspicious of the offer and of the papers she is asked to sign, she writes for advice to the leader of an emigre organisation she trusted long ago.
characters.name: Maria Ostrakova

characters.description: The Soviet official who approaches Ostrakova in Paris: nominally a trade or embassy functionary, effusive, sweating and oddly clumsy for a man on such an errand. He talks a great deal more than his business requires.
characters.name: Oleg Kirov

characters.description: An elderly Estonian, once a soldier and a Soviet officer and for decades afterwards the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London, run for years as a Circus agent and then dropped when the service reorganised. Poor, proud and still observing the tradecraft he was taught, he telephones his old service demanding to speak to the case officer he knew by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has something that concerns them all.
characters.name: General Vladimir

characters.description: Long retired from the Circus, living alone in Chelsea and sorting his papers, still married in name to Ann and still without her. He is fetched out at night to deal with the death of a former agent, on the understanding that his job is to tidy the matter away quietly. He is old, tired and out of practice, and the one man who understands what the dead man was trying to say.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: Smiley's wife, absent, living elsewhere with someone else, and still the fixed point of his private life. Her cigarette lighter and her infidelities both belong to the history that binds Smiley to his opponent.
characters.name: Ann Smiley

characters.description: The Cabinet Office official responsible for the intelligence services, anxious above all that an emigre killing in London should not become a political embarrassment. He wants the affair closed with a minimum of enquiry and turns to Smiley because Smiley can be disowned.
characters.name: Oliver Lacon

characters.description: A senior Circus administrator of the present regime, protective of procedure, budgets and his own position, who treats the dead man as an obsolete liability and Smiley as an awkwardness to be managed.
characters.name: Lauder Strickland

characters.description: A very young Circus duty officer who took the old man's telephone call and, having been taught nothing about the people the service used to run, handled it by the book. He is shaken by what followed and tells Smiley more than he is supposed to.
characters.name: Mostyn

characters.description: An Estonian exile who runs a Baltic emigre library and club in London, once the General's deputy and now the keeper of his organisation's dwindling affairs. Talkative, aggrieved and a considerable chess player, he gives his own version of the old man's last weeks.
characters.name: Mikhel

characters.description: A young Estonian lorry driver on the continental routes, the son of one of the General's old comrades, who ran errands for the old man out of family loyalty and without understanding what he was carrying. He is frightened and wants nothing more to do with any of it.
characters.name: Villem

characters.description: The Circus's former Soviet researcher, now seriously ill and living in the Norfolk countryside with her companion and her dogs, drinking and remembering. Her memory for Moscow Centre's people and their careers is still complete, and she has never stopped following the career of one officer in particular.
characters.name: Connie Sachs

characters.description: A stateless adventurer of Baltic origin, sometime prisoner, confidence man and agent for several services, who worked with the General for years. Charming, unreliable and physically brave, he lives in Hamburg and has been chasing a particular Soviet official for reasons of his own.
characters.name: Otto Leipzig

characters.description: A former Circus officer, now dealing in pictures in the West End under an assumed name and a foreign accent. Hungarian, adaptable and expert in surveillance and safe houses, he owes Smiley his freedom from prosecution and comes back to run a team for him without asking what the operation is for.
characters.name: Toby Esterhase

characters.description: A Hamburg nightclub proprietor and old associate of Otto Leipzig, discreet, businesslike and loyal to his friend. He keeps what Leipzig left with him and will hand it over only on the right terms.
characters.name: Claus Kretzschmar

characters.description: The commercial counsellor at the Soviet embassy in Bern, a pedantic, henpecked official with an academic manner, a wife who watches him and a mistress among the embassy staff. He performs, under orders from Moscow, a private duty outside all normal embassy business, and he is very frightened of it.
characters.name: Grigoriev

characters.description: A young Russian woman in a private Swiss clinic, disturbed, articulate and intermittently violent, held under a name and a nationality that are not hers. She does not know who is paying for her, and the accounts she gives of her own history contradict one another.
characters.name: Alexandra

recaps.ending: Grigoriev, broken by Toby's team and questioned by Smiley in a Bern safe flat, gives up the whole arrangement: the girl in the clinic is Karla's daughter, mentally ill, smuggled out of Russia under a false identity and a false nationality, and maintained in Switzerland with money embezzled from Moscow Centre's operational funds. Kirov was ordered to build the legend, talked too much to Otto Leipzig, and was recalled and shot; Vladimir, Leipzig and very nearly Ostrakova were killed to bury the same secret. Smiley now has what no professional lever could give him: the private crime for which Karla's own service would destroy him. He sends word to Moscow through the channel Karla built, offering him the choice between exposure and coming across. Karla comes. On a bridge in Berlin, watched by Smiley, Toby and the reception party, he crosses into the West, a small man carrying almost nothing, and as he passes he drops the cigarette lighter Smiley once gave him. Smiley has beaten him by using the one human attachment Karla had, exactly as Karla would have done, and the victory gives him nothing. He turns away, and when Toby tells him he has won he can barely agree.
recaps.in_short: In Paris an ageing Russian emigree, Ostrakova, is approached by a Soviet official offering to release the daughter she left behind, and writes for help to General Vladimir, an old Estonian exile in London and a discarded Circus agent. Vladimir tries to reach his former case officer under Moscow rules and is shot dead on Hampstead Heath. Smiley, long retired, is sent to tidy the death away quietly, and instead follows the trail the old man left: a hidden negative, an emigre courier, a Hamburg confidence man named Otto Leipzig, and photographs and a tape recording of the Soviet official's indiscretions. Reassembling his old people, Connie Sachs, Toby Esterhase, Guillam and Mendel, and working outside the service, Smiley establishes that Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, has been using Centre money and Centre officers to hide his mentally ill daughter in a Swiss clinic under a false identity. Everyone who learned of it has been killed. Smiley breaks the Soviet official who pays the clinic's bills, and uses the daughter to force Karla's defection. Karla crosses a Berlin bridge into the West, and Smiley takes no pleasure in it.

recaps.text: Previously: George Smiley spent his career in the Circus, Britain's secret intelligence service, and much of it against Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate. Karla recruited and ran Bill Haydon, who rose to the top of the Circus, betrayed its networks and its allies, wrecked the operation that left Jim Prideaux shot and imprisoned, and conducted an affair with Smiley's wife Ann on Karla's instructions to blunt Smiley's judgement. Brought back from retirement, Smiley identified and trapped Haydon and was left to rebuild the ruined service. Working backwards through what Haydon had suppressed, he then uncovered a Soviet payments operation in the Far East and traced it to Nelson Ko, an agent Karla had run inside China for twenty years; but the prize was taken over by the Americans and by Whitehall, the field man Jerry Westerby was killed, and Smiley was eased out of the chief's chair in favour of Saul Enderby. Smiley's marriage to Ann has not survived, and the two men's twenty-year contest has never been settled.

In Paris, Maria Ostrakova, an ageing Russian emigree, is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who says her daughter Alexandra, left behind in Russia many years earlier, may be allowed to join her if she signs certain papers. The interview frightens her: the man knows too much about her history and too little about her daughter, and the arrangement smells of something other than compassion. She writes to General Vladimir, the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London whom she trusted long ago. Vladimir, an old Estonian long since dropped by the Circus, telephones his former service demanding to see the case officer he knew only by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has proof of something big. A young duty officer handles the call by the book. Before any meeting can take place, Vladimir is shot dead on Hampstead Heath at night, his face destroyed by the second bullet, and George Smiley is fetched out of retirement to identify the body.

Lacon of the Cabinet Office and the Circus administrator Strickland want the killing disposed of as an emigre quarrel with no British connection, and give Smiley an unofficial commission to make the loose ends disappear. Smiley does the opposite. Going over the old man's route and lodgings, he finds what the killers missed: a cigarette packet left in the classic manner with a photographic negative concealed in it, the proof Vladimir was carrying to his meeting. He interviews the young duty officer, who repeats the old man's words; and Mikhel, the deputy at the emigre library, whose account is fluent and incomplete. He learns that Vladimir had recently sent a young Estonian courier abroad. The service, meanwhile, formally wants nothing to do with any of it, which leaves Smiley free to work alone.

The courier, a lorry driver named Villem, admits to a run to Hamburg where a stranger passed him an envelope on a train. Smiley goes to Norfolk to see Connie Sachs, dying and drinking in the country, who identifies the men in the story: Otto Leipzig, a Baltic adventurer and part-time agent who had worked with Vladimir for years, and Oleg Kirov, a Soviet official whose career and postings make no sense unless he was doing something outside embassy work. Connie also confirms whose directorate Kirov belonged to. In Hamburg, Smiley finds that Leipzig has been murdered, but recovers from Leipzig's associate Kretzschmar what the operation was for: a compromising photograph and a tape on which Kirov, drunk and boastful, describes having been ordered to find a suitable emigre identity for a girl, a piece of work no intelligence service would ever run in that way.

Smiley recruits his own people rather than the Circus's: Toby Esterhase, now selling pictures in the West End, brings a surveillance team; Peter Guillam helps from Paris; Mendel does the London work. In Paris, Ostrakova, who has been living in fear since the approach, is run down in the street and badly hurt, and survives; Smiley finds her and hears her account of Kirov's proposition and of the daughter she has not seen since infancy. The pattern is now clear. Kirov was building a false identity in the West for a young woman, using an emigree mother as the cover story, and everyone who came near the secret has been killed: Kirov himself recalled to Moscow and shot, then Vladimir and Leipzig. The operation was not run by Moscow Centre as an institution but by one man inside it, using its resources for a purpose of his own, and the trail leads to Switzerland.

In Bern, Toby's team identifies the man who does the paying: Grigoriev, the Soviet embassy's commercial counsellor, a fussy, unhappy official who makes regular private journeys to a discreet clinic in the countryside and hands over large sums in cash. In the clinic is a disturbed young Russian woman, registered under a name and a nationality that are not hers, who does not know who is responsible for her. Smiley has the watchers document every movement, then has Grigoriev taken quietly and confronted in a safe flat with what has been observed: the money, the false papers, his mistress, and the certainty that his own service would treat all of it as a capital matter. Grigoriev, terrified and relieved to be able to speak, begins to explain who ordered him to do it and why.

Grigoriev's account completes the case: the girl in the clinic is Karla's own daughter, mentally ill, taken out of Russia under an invented identity and kept in Switzerland with money stolen from Moscow Centre's operational funds. It is the one act for which Karla's own service would destroy him, and it is why Kirov, Vladimir and Leipzig died and why Ostrakova was to have died. Smiley sends Karla the choice through the channel Karla himself built: come over, or be exposed to Moscow. Then he waits in Berlin. On a winter night Karla walks across the bridge into the West, a small, ordinary man carrying nothing, and as he passes Smiley he drops the cigarette lighter that Smiley had given him twenty years earlier in an Indian jail. Smiley has won by doing exactly what his opponent would have done, using a sick girl and a frightened official as instruments, and he leaves the bridge with no sense of triumph at all.

characters.description: Fourteen, and pulled out of the sea off the Australian coast after falling back to Earth from orbit. He is exhausted, a long way from home and, for once, in the hands of a service that has no file on him and no claim over him. That does not last.
characters.name: Alex Rider

characters.description: A senior officer of the Australian Secret Intelligence Service, direct and persuasive, who has been trying for years to get somebody inside the people-smuggling networks that run through Southeast Asia. He knows precisely who Alex is by the time they meet, and he has a proposal ready.
characters.name: Ethan Brooke

characters.description: A former MI6 officer, now with the Australian service, who turns out to be Alex's godfather. He worked alongside John and Helen Rider, was there the night Alex's life changed, and carries a bad old wound in his stomach from it. He is the first person Alex has met who knew his parents as people rather than as files, and he is to travel with Alex as his minder.
characters.name: Ash

characters.description: The head of a snakehead operating out of Bangkok, half English and half Chinese, educated at an English public school and impeccably polite about it. He suffers from a bone disease that makes his skeleton brittle, so he moves carefully and is never without protection, and he runs a business that moves human beings as freight and sells whatever is left of them.
characters.name: Major Winston Yu

characters.description: The MI6 agent Alex first met under the codename Fox during Special Air Service selection training. Young, capable and one of the few people in the service who treats Alex as a colleague, he arrives as part of the operation's back-up.
characters.name: Ben Daniels

characters.description: The deputy head of MI6 Special Operations, who knows more about what happened to Alex's parents than she has ever been willing to say.
characters.name: Mrs Jones

recaps.ending: The bomb is stopped: Alex prevents Royal Blue from triggering the landslide, no wave is generated, and the conference and the coastline are never hit. Major Winston Yu does not survive the operation, and the snakehead's network is broken open. The harder ending is Ash. Alex learns that his godfather was the traitor inside the operation years ago, the man Scorpia paid to betray John Rider and to make sure the Riders' plane came down; Alex's parents died because Ash sold them. Ash is fatally injured during the fighting, and dies having admitted it, leaving Alex with a truth that nobody else needs and no one to be angry at. Alex goes home to London knowing exactly how his mother and father died and who arranged it, having been used again by a service that is not even his own, and having been closer to being killed on an operating table than in any firefight. Scorpia, whose contract set the whole thing in motion, remains in business.
recaps.in_short: Fished out of the sea off Australia after his fall from orbit, Alex is recruited by the Australian Secret Intelligence Service to go into the snakeheads, the gangs that smuggle people across Southeast Asia. He is teamed with Ash, a former MI6 officer who turns out to be his godfather and who knew his parents. Posing as refugees, the two are moved along the smuggling route to a camp where the gang's other trade becomes clear: those who cannot pay are taken to an illegal clinic and stripped for organs, and Alex is nearly killed on the table. Captured, he is brought before Major Winston Yu, who runs the operation and has taken a contract from Scorpia called Royal Blue: a bomb sunk at an unstable point on the seabed to trigger an underwater landslide and a wave that would destroy an international aid conference and the coast around it. Alex stops the detonation and Yu is killed. He also learns that Ash was the traitor who betrayed his parents to Scorpia; Ash dies admitting it.

recaps.text: Previously: Alex Rider, fourteen, was recruited by MI6 after his uncle Ian's murder and used repeatedly by Alan Blunt and Mrs Jones. He stopped Herod Sayle's poisoned school computers, broke Dr Hugo Grief's cloning operation at Point Blanc, survived General Alexei Sarov, and prevented Damian Cray from launching stolen American missiles; the dying assassin Yassen Gregorovich sent him to Venice, where Scorpia's Julia Rothman recruited him with a lie about his father before he discovered the organisation meant to murder thousands of London schoolchildren and destroyed its weapon. MI6 then told him the truth: John Rider had been their own officer, working inside Scorpia under the codename Hunter, and his execution was staged to bring him out. Alex's parents died soon afterwards when a bomb brought down their plane. Scorpia's answer to Alex was a sniper's bullet in the chest. Most recently, the billionaire Nikolai Drevin tried to bring his own space station down on Washington; Alex diverted it and fell back to Earth into the sea off Australia.

Alex comes down in the ocean off the Australian coast and is picked up alive. Instead of being sent straight home he is passed to the Australian Secret Intelligence Service, whose senior officer Ethan Brooke has a proposal. The service has spent years failing to get anyone inside the snakeheads, the gangs that move people illegally across Southeast Asia and treat them as cargo, and a boy travelling with an adult would be exactly the kind of pair the route swallows without comment. The adult offered to Alex is Ash: a former MI6 officer, now working in Australia, who was a friend and colleague of John and Helen Rider and who is Alex's godfather. It is the first time Alex has met anybody who knew his parents personally.

Alex and Ash go in as a father and son with no money and no papers, and are handed along the snakehead's chain from Bangkok southward. Ash talks, guardedly, about the Riders, and about the night Alex's life changed and the wound he still carries from it, but there is a great deal he will not say. The journey itself is worse than either of them expected: the people around them have paid everything they have for a passage that treats them as freight, the handlers are casual about who arrives and who does not, and there is no way to leave the route once you are on it.

The route ends not in a new country but at a holding camp, and there Alex discovers the snakehead's second trade. Those who cannot pay the rest of their passage are taken to an illegal clinic run for the organisation, where they are used as a source of organs for buyers who ask no questions. Alex is identified as a healthy donor and taken to the table, and comes closer to being killed there than in any operation he has run. He gets off it and out of the camp, but he can no longer pretend to be a refugee, and the people running the network now know that somebody has been inside it.

Alex is taken to Major Winston Yu, who owns the snakehead: a courteous, English-educated man whose bones are so brittle that a fall would cripple him, and who describes his business as logistics. Yu is not working for himself. Scorpia has bought his network for an operation called Royal Blue, and the target is an international aid conference being held off the Australian coast, where the people the client wants dead will be gathered in one place. The method is geological. A bomb sunk at a precise point on the seabed will bring down an unstable shelf, and the wave it raises will do the killing, leaving a natural disaster and no assassin to find.

The bomb is already in place on a disused offshore platform, with the timing set and the conference assembling. Alex reaches the rig with the operation's back-up, including Ben Daniels, the MI6 agent he first knew as Fox at the SAS training camp. In the fighting on the platform Alex stops the detonation; there is no landslide and no wave, the conference and the coast are untouched, and Major Yu does not survive. The snakehead's network is broken open, though Scorpia, which commissioned the whole thing, is not touched at all.

The last thing Alex learns is the worst. Ash was the traitor. Years earlier, in the operation that ended his own career, he took Scorpia's money and gave them John Rider, and it was Ash who made sure the plane carrying Alex's parents came down. His godfather is the reason Alex grew up without them. Ash is fatally injured in the fighting on the rig and dies having admitted all of it, leaving Alex holding a confession nobody else has any use for. Alex goes home to London knowing exactly how his mother and father died and who arranged it, having been lent out, used and very nearly killed by a service that was not even his own.

characters.description: A Japanese American fisherman on trial for the murder of Carl Heine. Kabuo is a husband and father whose rigid stillness in court gives observers little indication of what he is thinking.
characters.name: Kabuo Miyamoto

characters.description: Kabuo's wife, seated behind him during the trial. Hatsue is composed and attentive as she follows the proceedings that will decide whether her husband returns to their family.
characters.name: Hatsue Miyamoto

characters.description: The editor and sole reporter of the island newspaper, attending Kabuo's trial as both journalist and local observer. A wounded veteran who lost an arm in the war, Ishmael is watchful and emotionally withdrawn.
characters.name: Ishmael Chambers

characters.description: The dead fisherman whose body was pulled from his own net. Carl was a large, quiet islander, a husband and father, and an experienced seaman whose apparent drowning begins to look suspicious.
characters.name: Carl Heine Jr.

characters.description: San Piedro's sheriff, responsible for investigating Carl Heine's death. Art is methodical and generally decent, but the unusual wound on Carl's head and other circumstantial clues lead him to treat the drowning as a possible homicide.
characters.name: Art Moran

characters.description: Carl's widow and the mother of his children. Grieving but direct, Susan Marie helps Sheriff Moran establish her husband's habits and movements around the time of his death.
characters.name: Susan Marie Heine

characters.description: The prosecutor in Kabuo's trial. Hooks builds a case from physical traces, the Miyamoto family's land grievance, and Kabuo's initial lack of candor, presenting separate pieces of circumstantial evidence as a single deliberate killing.
characters.name: Alvin Hooks

characters.description: Kabuo's elderly defense attorney. Gudmundsson challenges the prosecution's assumptions and warns the jury against allowing racial stereotypes or Kabuo's controlled expression to substitute for proof.
characters.name: Nels Gudmundsson

characters.description: The island coroner, who examines Carl's body. Whaley identifies a head injury that occurred before the drowning and recognizes that its shape could be consistent with a forceful blow, an observation that helps turn an apparent fishing accident into a murder inquiry.
characters.name: Horace Whaley

characters.description: Carl's mother, a stern woman who never accepted the Miyamoto family's claim on land once owned by the Heines. During the wartime removal, she used the missed payments to end the Miyamotos' purchase agreement and later sold the farm elsewhere.
characters.name: Etta Heine

characters.description: Kabuo's father, who arranged to buy strawberry acreage from Carl Heine Sr. and improved it while making payments. The wartime incarceration of his family prevented him from completing the agreement, leaving Kabuo determined to recover what he regards as the family's land.
characters.name: Zenhichi Miyamoto

characters.description: Ishmael's late father and the former editor of the island newspaper. Arthur reported firmly against anti-Japanese agitation and taught his son that a local newspaper owes its community fairness as well as facts.
characters.name: Arthur Chambers

recaps.ending: Ishmael finds records from the lighthouse radio station showing that a freighter passed San Piedro during the fogbound night of Carl's death. Its wake, arriving during a local power failure, explains how Carl could have been knocked from his boat after climbing the mast to deal with his lantern. The evidence supports Kabuo's account of helping Carl with a dead battery and then leaving him alive. Ishmael initially sits alone with information that can save the husband of the woman he still loves, but Hatsue's appeal to his better nature ends his hesitation. He gives her the records, and she takes them to Sheriff Moran. The authorities confirm the accident and the charge against Kabuo is dismissed before the jury delivers a verdict. Kabuo returns to Hatsue and their children. Hatsue remains grateful to Ishmael but does not renew their youthful romance; her life is with Kabuo. By choosing truth over resentment, Ishmael begins to move beyond the grievance that has governed his postwar life and writes the full account of Carl's accidental death.
recaps.in_short: In 1954, Japanese American fisherman Kabuo Miyamoto stands trial on San Piedro Island for killing fellow fisherman Carl Heine. The prosecution links a head wound, blood and a disputed boat battery to an old conflict over strawberry land that Kabuo's family lost while incarcerated during World War II. The trial draws out the island's buried history: prejudice against its Japanese American residents, Kabuo's war service, and newspaper editor Ishmael Chambers's secret youthful love for Kabuo's wife, Hatsue. Kabuo eventually explains that he found Carl disabled at sea, helped him install a spare battery, discussed buying back the family acreage, and left him alive. Ishmael discovers lighthouse records proving that a freighter's wake could have knocked Carl from his mast during a power failure. After briefly withholding the evidence, Ishmael gives it to Hatsue. The accident is confirmed, Kabuo is freed, and Ishmael finally acts according to the fairness his father taught him rather than the bitterness he has carried since the war and Hatsue's rejection.

recaps.text: A winter storm surrounds the courthouse on San Piedro Island as Kabuo Miyamoto, a Japanese American fisherman, goes on trial for murdering Carl Heine Jr. Carl's body had been found caught in his own fishing net after his boat was discovered drifting. Sheriff Art Moran's investigation showed that Carl suffered a serious head injury before drowning, making an ordinary accident seem doubtful. The courtroom brings together people whose histories are deeply connected: Kabuo's wife Hatsue; Ishmael Chambers, the island newspaper editor and a wounded war veteran; Carl's widow Susan Marie; and the attorneys Alvin Hooks and Nels Gudmundsson. From the outset, the case rests on interpretation as much as direct evidence. Kabuo's controlled expression looks suspicious to some observers, while his defense insists that reserve and ancestry are not proof of violence.

The coroner testifies that Carl's head wound was inflicted before he entered the water and could match a forceful strike. Investigators also focus on a battery associated with Carl's boat and on physical traces that may place Kabuo aboard it. The prosecution begins arranging these facts into a theory of murder, although no witness saw Carl die. Alongside the courtroom evidence, the story returns to Ishmael and Hatsue's childhood. They grew close while young but concealed the relationship because Hatsue expected her family and the island to reject it. Their private bond gives Ishmael's coverage of the trial a personal stake he cannot acknowledge publicly. Hatsue is now committed to Kabuo and their children, while Ishmael's wartime injury and unresolved longing have left him detached from much of island life.

The alleged motive reaches back to land. Kabuo's father, Zenhichi, had made payments to Carl Heine Sr. for strawberry acreage and worked the property for years. When the government removed the island's Japanese American families during World War II, the Miyamotos could no longer maintain the agreement. Etta Heine ended the arrangement and later sold the farm to another buyer. Kabuo returned from military service believing that his family had been deprived of land they had nearly paid for, and he continued trying to recover it. The trial also exposes how readily old racial hostility can color neutral facts. Ishmael remembers his father Arthur using the island newspaper to oppose such prejudice. Those memories sharpen the contrast between the public duty Ishmael inherited and the private resentment he still carries toward Hatsue.

The past of the principal witnesses becomes inseparable from the trial. Hatsue's family was sent away from the island and eventually confined at Manzanar. Under pressure from her family, her own doubts, and the upheaval of removal, she ended her hidden relationship with Ishmael and later married Kabuo. Both men then fought in the war: Ishmael returned missing an arm, and Kabuo returned burdened by what he had done as a soldier. Carl likewise came home changed. The prosecution treats Kabuo's land grievance and martial skill as evidence of a planned attack, while the defense argues that war, reserve, and anger do not establish murder. Testimony about the boats and the blood evidence strengthens the circumstantial case, but the exact sequence on the water remains unknown.

Kabuo explains why he initially concealed part of the night from Sheriff Moran. He says he encountered Carl at sea with a dead battery and supplied a compatible spare. While the men worked aboard Carl's boat, Kabuo cut his hand, accounting for his blood there. They also spoke about the Heine acreage, and Carl agreed in principle to sell Kabuo the portion his family had once sought. Kabuo then left Carl alive. He withheld the meeting because he understood how the land dispute, his presence on the boat, and local prejudice would make the truth sound like a murder story. His testimony offers an innocent explanation for the physical evidence, but it also asks the jury to believe a defendant who was not candid at the start. As the lawyers prepare their final arguments, Ishmael investigates the weather and maritime communications from the night Carl died.

The lawyers complete their arguments and the jury begins considering a case with no eyewitness to Carl's death. Ishmael, searching records at the lighthouse radio station, discovers that a freighter passed the island during the relevant period. Its wake reached the fishing grounds during a power failure, providing a coherent explanation for Carl's fatal head injury and fall: after Kabuo departed, Carl climbed his mast to deal with his lantern and was thrown by the unexpected swell. Ishmael takes the records but at first tells no one. Keeping silent could condemn Kabuo and preserve Ishmael's private hold on Hatsue's suffering. When Hatsue asks him to help, he finally rejects that impulse and gives her the evidence. Sheriff Moran verifies the new account, and the murder charge is dismissed before a verdict. Kabuo is reunited with his family. Hatsue does not return Ishmael's romantic hopes, but his decision breaks with years of self-pity and honors the journalistic integrity his father modeled. He records Carl's death as the accident the evidence shows it to have been.

characters.description: An elderly woman looking back on her life in nineteenth-century Hunan. As a girl from a modest farming family, Lily learns that the quality of her feet may give her an unusually favorable marriage. She is disciplined, eager to be worthy of love, and deeply shaped by the rules that confine women to domestic spaces and judge them through obedience, marriage, and sons.
characters.name: Lily

characters.description: The girl matched to Lily as her laotong, a formal lifelong counterpart meant to share an intimate bond deeper than ordinary friendship. Snow Flower appears refined and comes from a family believed to have higher standing than Lily's. Through messages written in nüshu, she gives Lily companionship and a private language for feelings their public lives do not permit.
characters.name: Snow Flower

characters.description: The matchmaker who recognizes that Lily's feet could transform her marriage prospects. Madame Wang arranges both Lily's laotong relationship with Snow Flower and the negotiations that will determine Lily's future household. She is worldly, authoritative, and one of the few women able to move regularly between otherwise separate families.
characters.name: Madame Wang

characters.description: Lily's mother, who prepares her daughters for the narrow duties expected of women. She supervises Lily's footbinding with severe resolve, believing that enduring pain and achieving the proper shape are necessary for her daughter's security and the family's advancement.
characters.name: Lily's mother

characters.description: Lily's cousin and childhood companion, close enough in age that they pass through footbinding and preparation for marriage together. Beautiful Moon shares the women's upstairs world with Lily and gives her an ordinary family friendship alongside the more formal bond with Snow Flower.
characters.name: Beautiful Moon

characters.description: Lily's younger sister, whose feet are bound with Lily's and Beautiful Moon's. Her body cannot withstand the infection that follows, showing Lily at an early age that the custom demanded as a condition of womanhood can also be fatal.
characters.name: Third Sister

characters.description: The man chosen as Lily's husband in the prosperous Lu family of Tongkou. At their marriage he is still largely a stranger to her, and their relationship is governed by family duty and the expectation that Lily will produce sons and serve his household.
characters.name: Lily's husband

characters.description: The senior woman in Lily's married household. Lady Lu evaluates the new bride according to her feet, manners, work, fertility, and obedience. Her approval carries immense weight as Lily learns the hierarchy of the wealthy family she has entered.
characters.name: Lady Lu

characters.description: Snow Flower's husband, a butcher whose trade places his family low in the local social order. His household is far poorer and harsher than the one Snow Flower's upbringing led Lily to expect, and his temper adds fear to the difficulties Snow Flower faces as a wife and mother.
characters.name: Snow Flower's husband

characters.description: Snow Flower's mother, once associated with a cultivated household but weakened by addiction and the family's decline. Her circumstances are part of the truth Snow Flower has been ashamed to tell Lily and help explain the difference between the girl's polished education and her actual marriage prospects.
characters.name: Snow Flower's mother

recaps.ending: After publicly condemning Snow Flower, Lily learns that she misunderstood her friend's message: Snow Flower's sworn sisters had offered companionship during suffering, not replaced the laotong bond. By then Snow Flower is gravely ill. Lily goes to her, nurses her through her final days, and hears how loneliness, abuse, poverty, and the deaths of her children shaped the choices Lily judged so harshly. Snow Flower dies with their attachment restored but without giving Lily the absolution she wants. Lily assumes responsibility for Snow Flower's surviving children and later hears further testimony from the women who had supported her. In old age, socially honored but burdened by remorse, Lily writes the history of their relationship and addresses Snow Flower's spirit. The fan preserves their nüshu messages, including evidence of Lily's failures as well as their love, and Lily asks forgiveness for having valued pride and social rules above a faithful understanding of her friend.
recaps.in_short: In nineteenth-century Hunan, Lily's carefully bound feet bring her a prestigious marriage and a formal laotong match with Snow Flower. The girls communicate in women's nüshu writing, especially on a fan, and promise lifelong devotion. Lily rises into a wealthy household, while Snow Flower reveals that her family has fallen and that she must marry an abusive butcher. Marriage, childbirth, poverty, and the Taiping upheaval widen the difference between their lives. During a dangerous mountain refuge, Snow Flower suffers another devastating loss. Later she writes of sworn sisters who comfort her; Lily reads this as rejection, publicly denounces her, and breaks their bond. She discovers too late that Snow Flower never meant to replace her. Lily nurses Snow Flower as she dies, cares for her children, and spends the rest of her life regretting that pride and convention made her fail the person she loved most.

recaps.text: From old age, Lily recalls growing up in a farming household in Hunan, where a girl's value is tied to marriage, obedience, and the sons she may bear. A visiting matchmaker, Madame Wang, decides Lily has feet capable of an exceptional result and recommends a binding schedule that may raise her above the marriage normally expected for her family. Lily, her cousin Beautiful Moon, and Third Sister begin the prolonged process together under the women's supervision. The pain is treated as necessary discipline. Third Sister develops a fatal infection, but Lily continues, driven by her mother's demands and the promise that success will secure her future. Madame Wang also proposes an unusual honor: Lily may be formally paired with a laotong, a girl of the same age whose matched qualities will make them lifelong counterparts.

Lily is matched with Snow Flower, a poised girl believed to come from a superior family. Their first message arrives on a fan in nüshu, the women's script used to exchange private thoughts within lives controlled by men and senior relatives. The girls visit, learn one another's habits, and promise a bond that will outlast marriage and physical separation. Snow Flower's polish introduces Lily to customs beyond her village, while Lily offers wholehearted loyalty. Through letters and shared festivals they grow emotionally inseparable. Madame Wang's prediction about Lily is also fulfilled: her bound feet and conduct secure a marriage into the wealthy Lu family in Tongkou. The match promises status but means that Lily must eventually leave her natal home and prove herself among strangers.

Lily enters the Lu household in the enclosed bridal chair and begins married life under Lady Lu's scrutiny. Her position improves as she meets domestic expectations and begins to bear children, especially sons. Snow Flower's situation proves painfully different from the image surrounding their match. Her family has declined, her mother is addicted to opium, and Snow Flower has been married to a butcher, a low-status trade associated with blood and death. Her husband is volatile and their household lives close to poverty. Lily feels deceived by the concealment but continues the laotong relationship. Their meetings and messages now cross an increasing social distance: Lily is becoming an honored wife, while Snow Flower faces hunger, fear, and repeated uncertainty about her children's survival.

The women's adult lives are defined by pregnancies, births, illness, and the demands of their husbands' families. Lily's production of sons strengthens her authority in the Lu household. Snow Flower loses children and endures her husband's anger, yet she often minimizes her suffering when writing to Lily. The Taiping conflict then drives both families from their homes. They shelter in the mountains through brutal winter conditions with little food or protection. Social distinctions offer limited defense against cold, violence, and disease. Snow Flower suffers another devastating loss, and Lily struggles to respond with the tenderness their old promises require. Although they survive and return from the mountains, grief and the unequal shape of their lives have placed strain inside a bond both women once believed unbreakable.

Now an influential woman in her community, Lily increasingly applies the standards of her prosperous household to Snow Flower's choices. When Snow Flower writes that a group of sworn sisters has comforted her, Lily interprets the message as a declaration that their exclusive laotong bond has been discarded. Hurt pride turns into punishment. Lily composes a formal condemnation and repeats her grievances publicly, exposing Snow Flower's private failures and isolating her further. Only afterward does Lily learn that the sworn sisters supplemented rather than replaced Snow Flower's devotion and that they were present when Lily was not. Snow Flower becomes gravely ill. Confronted with the damage caused by her certainty, Lily returns to her former companion, but illness has made time for repair very short.

Lily nurses Snow Flower and listens as the hidden extent of her friend's suffering becomes clear. Snow Flower dies after the two acknowledge their enduring love, leaving Lily reconciled but unable to undo her public betrayal. Lily takes responsibility for Snow Flower's surviving children and speaks with the sworn sisters, who explain how faithfully Snow Flower continued to think of her. Decades later, Lily has achieved the position once promised by her excellent feet: she is a respected elder surrounded by descendants. That success cannot erase her remorse. She records the women's story in nüshu and preserves the fan that carried their messages across childhood, marriage, war, estrangement, and death. Addressing Snow Flower beyond the grave, Lily asks forgiveness and recognizes that rigid ideas of duty kept her from fully hearing the person to whom she had pledged her life.

characters.description: A Turkish poet who has spent twelve years in political exile in Germany. Quiet, solitary, and uncertain of his convictions, he travels to the eastern city of Kars to report on municipal elections and the suicides of young women forbidden to wear headscarves at school.
characters.name: Ka

characters.description: Ka's former university acquaintance, now living at her father's hotel in Kars after separating from Muhtar. Beautiful and self-possessed, she becomes the focus of Ka's hope for a new life outside Turkey.
characters.name: İpek

characters.description: İpek's younger sister, a confident woman associated with the headscarf movement. She resists efforts by secular authorities to dictate how religious women should appear in public.
characters.name: Kadife

characters.description: İpek's former husband and a candidate for mayor with an Islamist party. Once part of Ka's secular intellectual circle, he has returned to religious belief while remaining painfully conscious of his own failures.
characters.name: Muhtar

characters.description: İpek and Kadife's father, a retired leftist who lives with his daughters at the Snow Palace Hotel. He follows Kars's political turmoil closely and retains the habits of an older secular opposition.
characters.name: Turgut Bey

characters.description: The editor of Kars's local newspaper. He operates in a climate where rumor, official pressure, and prediction can shape the news before events have happened.
characters.name: Serdar Bey

characters.description: A charismatic underground Islamist wanted by the authorities. Admired by younger believers, he opposes both the secular state's coercion and simplistic uses of religion for political theater.
characters.name: Blue

characters.description: A religious high-school student with an intense, questioning mind. He talks to Ka about faith, doubt, love, and fear with an openness that makes a strong impression on the poet.
characters.name: Necip

characters.description: Necip's close friend and fellow student. He shares Necip's religious world and his feelings for Kadife, but is quieter and more guarded when he first meets Ka.
characters.name: Fazıl

characters.description: An actor and committed secularist who once toured provincial Turkey with his theatrical company. In Kars he plans a live performance designed to turn the city's political conflicts into public spectacle.
characters.name: Sunay Zaim

characters.description: Sunay's wife and leading actress, an experienced performer who shares his secular political commitments. She helps turn their Kars production into an intervention in the city's conflict.
characters.name: Funda Eser

characters.description: A local religious leader whom Ka visits while investigating the city's suicides and his own uncertain relationship to belief. His influence reaches people who feel excluded from the official secular order.
characters.name: Sheikh Saadettin

characters.description: The novelist who reconstructs Ka's final years after his death. He follows Ka's route through Kars, interviews the people who knew him, and tries to recover a lost cycle of poems.
characters.name: Orhan

recaps.ending: Ka arranges a bargain in which Kadife will bare her head during Sunay's televised play in exchange for Blue's release. Blue is freed, but security forces track him to a hiding place and kill him; evidence later convinces İpek that Ka revealed the location. Onstage, Kadife removes her headscarf and fires what she believes has become a harmless theatrical weapon, but the gun is loaded and Sunay dies. With the roads open, Ka prepares to leave Kars with İpek. After learning of his part in Blue's death, she refuses to join him. Ka returns alone to Frankfurt and spends four isolated years there before he is shot dead, apparently in revenge for Blue. His green notebook and the completed poems he called Snow cannot be found. Years later, Orhan retraces Ka's movements in Kars, interviews the survivors, and fails to recover the poems, leaving Ka's lost work and motives open to competing memories.
recaps.in_short: Ka, a poet exiled in Germany, travels through a snowstorm to Kars to report on an election and the suicides of young women pressured to remove their headscarves. He also hopes to reunite with İpek, a former acquaintance. Isolated by snow, the city becomes the site of a theatrical military coup led by actor Sunay Zaim, whose soldiers kill religious students during a live broadcast. Amid arrests and negotiations among secularists, Islamists, Kurdish activists, and state agents, Ka experiences a burst of poems that he arranges as a snowflake. He dreams that İpek will return to Germany with him but conceals information and mediates a bargain involving İpek's sister Kadife and the Islamist Blue. Blue is released and then killed after Ka reveals his location. Kadife unveils during a televised play and kills Sunay with a loaded gun. İpek learns of Ka's betrayal and stays in Kars. Ka returns alone to Frankfurt, where he is murdered four years later; his friend Orhan cannot recover the lost poems.

recaps.text: The poet Ka returns to Turkey after twelve years in Germany and travels by bus through heavy snow to the remote city of Kars. He claims to be reporting on a municipal election and on several young women who died by suicide after pressure over wearing headscarves, but he also hopes to see İpek, a former university acquaintance. Kars is poor, politically tense, and increasingly cut off as the storm closes the roads. Ka visits the local newspaper and begins interviewing families connected to the deaths. He also sees İpek at the Snow Palace Hotel run by her family and learns that she has separated from Muhtar, now an Islamist candidate for mayor. The possibility that she might love him gives Ka a private purpose beyond journalism.

Ka moves among groups that describe the suicides and the headscarf dispute in incompatible ways. Officials defend secular authority, religious students describe humiliation and exclusion, and families resist having private grief turned into political evidence. He visits Sheikh Saadettin and discovers that his years of political secularism have not resolved his desire to believe. He meets İpek's sister Kadife, who has become a prominent figure among the headscarf girls, and speaks with students Necip and Fazıl about faith, doubt, and love. Ka also encounters Blue, a charismatic underground Islamist sought by the state. During these meetings poems begin arriving in Ka's mind after years of silence, and he writes them into a green notebook.

Actor Sunay Zaim and his company stage a political play that is broadcast live across Kars. What begins as provocative theater becomes a coup when soldiers fire into the audience, killing religious students, including Necip. With the roads still blocked by snow, Sunay and allied security forces seize control, arrest Islamists, and search for Blue. Ka is drawn into the new regime's movements through the city while continuing to write poems and pursue İpek. The deaths trouble him, yet the closed world of Kars also gives him an intense sense that private happiness may still be possible. His conversations, dreams, and memories begin to fit a snowflake diagram whose branches represent reason, imagination, and memory.

Under the coup, prisoners are interrogated and rival political factions try to control how the city's events will be presented. Ka moves between Sunay's circle and the underground figures who distrust it, carrying messages because both sides see him as useful. He learns more about the ties among Blue, Kadife, and İpek, and his jealousy complicates his claim to neutrality. Sunay wants Kadife to appear in a final televised play and remove her headscarf as a dramatic symbol of secular liberation. Blue and Kadife refuse to let the act become a coerced victory for the state. Ka begins negotiating a bargain while assuring İpek that they can leave together for Frankfurt once the snow clears.

Ka helps formulate an agreement: Kadife will perform and unveil voluntarily if Blue is released. He seeks guarantees from Sunay and brings written assurances among the parties, while his own strongest concern remains whether İpek will go to Germany with him. Blue leaves custody, but the security services locate his hiding place and kill him. Ka's movements and the information he possesses create suspicion that he enabled them to find Blue. İpek, who has a deeper history with Blue than Ka wanted to acknowledge, begins to reassess Ka's promises and motives. The coup approaches its planned theatrical conclusion as the weather improves and the reopening of the roads threatens to end Sunay's brief control of Kars.

Kadife takes the stage in Sunay's televised play and removes her headscarf. She then shoots Sunay with a gun that is supposed to be part of the performance, but it contains live ammunition and kills him. The roads reopen as outside authority returns. Ka expects İpek to depart with him, but she learns that he disclosed Blue's whereabouts to the security forces and refuses to leave Kars. Ka returns alone to Frankfurt, where he lives unhappily for four years before being murdered, apparently by someone avenging Blue. His poems and green notebook disappear. The narrator Orhan later visits Frankfurt and Kars to reconstruct Ka's life and find the lost poems. He gathers conflicting memories but cannot restore the completed collection, and his account ends with Kars's residents conscious that an outsider will turn them into a story they cannot control.

aliases: His Grace, the Duke of Ankh
characters.description: Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and, by marriage, Duke of Ankh, a rank he has never become reconciled to. A copper by instinct and conviction, suspicious of privilege, including his own, and grimly aware of how much anger he keeps under control. He is a devoted, awkward father who reads his small son a bedtime story every night without fail, and he is about to be removed from the city and the job for the first time in his adult life.
characters.name: Sam Vimes

characters.description: The Patrician of Ankh-Morpork, who governs by knowing exactly what people will do and arranging matters accordingly. He has taken an interest in the idea of Commander Vimes being sent somewhere with no crime in it.
characters.name: Lord Vetinari

characters.description: Vimes's wife: an aristocrat by birth, a dragon breeder by enthusiasm, and immovable once she has decided what is good for her family. She has inherited a large country estate and has determined that her husband is going to take a holiday on it.
characters.name: Lady Sybil

characters.description: Vimes's six-year-old son, cheerful, observant, and currently engrossed in a natural history of animal droppings, a subject he can discuss at any length and in any company.
characters.name: Young Sam

characters.description: The Vimes household's gentleman's gentleman: impeccably correct, quietly amused, and equipped with a past on the streets that he has never entirely put down. He carries useful things in his hat and is a great deal more dangerous than any butler needs to be.
characters.name: Willikins

characters.description: The landlord of the village pub, an incomer with a professional welcome and a very good memory for faces, who recognizes Vimes rather faster than a country publican should. He knows a good deal about what happens locally and is careful about which parts of it he mentions.
characters.name: Jiminy

characters.description: A retired officer among the local gentry, straight-backed, courteous, and rather more troubled by the district's arrangements than his neighbours are. He has old-fashioned ideas about honour that his acquaintances find inconvenient.
characters.name: Colonel Makepeace

characters.description: The young local chief constable, the third generation of his family to hold the post, with no training, no colleagues, and a rule book he has largely worked out for himself. Earnest, badly out of his depth, and braver than his situation deserves.
characters.name: Feeney Upshot

characters.description: A goblin who attaches himself to Vimes: filthy, evil-smelling, sardonic, and entirely unbothered by either fact. He knows the country, the caves, and the river better than anyone alive, and turns up whenever Vimes is about to need him.
characters.name: Stinky

characters.description: A writer of children's books who lives locally and is regarded by the county as an eccentric. She has spent years among the goblins, has learned their language and their beliefs, and teaches those who will learn, which the neighbourhood considers at best foolish.
characters.name: Miss Felicity Beedle

characters.description: A young goblin woman living in the caves above the estate, taught music by Miss Beedle, who plays the harp with a skill that is impossible to explain away. What she can do is an argument in itself about what goblins are.
characters.name: Tears of the Mushroom

characters.description: A local man who works as an enforcer for people with money: fast, capable, and entirely without hesitation, and unusual even among killers in that he seems to feel nothing about it at all.
characters.name: Stratford

characters.description: A veteran Ankh-Morpork Watch sergeant of limited ambition and considerable seniority, who handles an item of goblin property in the course of a routine inquiry and begins, slowly and frighteningly, to stop being himself.
characters.name: Sergeant Colon

characters.description: A six-inch-tall Watch officer who was raised by gnomes and does the jobs no full-sized copper can, going into places nobody thinks to guard. He is a formidable fighter and is beginning to have questions about where he actually came from.
characters.name: Wee Mad Arthur

recaps.ending: Vimes proves the case: local landowners, with money and a name behind them, have been shipping goblins abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations and running smuggled goods on the same boats, and a young goblin woman was murdered to keep it quiet. Stratford, the killer, makes a last attempt on Vimes and on his family, and is taken; the aristocrat who financed the trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that leave him with nothing. The captured goblins are freed, Sergeant Colon recovers once the goblin pot he was carrying is returned to its owners, and the young country constable Feeney Upshot finishes the case as a real policeman with a future in the Watch. The decisive stroke is not an arrest: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork's Opera House, in front of the city's wealthy and powerful, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp, and an audience that had always been told goblins were vermin sits and listens to one make music. On the strength of that, and of the case Vimes has built, the law changes and goblins become people, with the rights that follow. Vimes goes home to the city and the job, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, as everyone including his wife expected, into police work.
recaps.in_short: Sam Vimes, Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and reluctant Duke of Ankh, is made to take a holiday at his wife's country estate, where he finds that a copper is still a copper. The district's goblins are treated as vermin, which under local law they are, and a young goblin woman has been murdered. The local chief constable, a young man named Feeney Upshot, arrests Vimes for it; Vimes turns him into a deputy instead, and together they uncover a trade run by the county's own gentry, shipping goblins abroad as slaves and smuggling goods on the return leg, with a professional killer named Stratford enforcing it. Vimes pursues the boats downriver through a flood, is nearly killed, and brings the evidence and the survivors back. The case ends not only in arrests but in a change of the law: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork a goblin girl plays the harp for the city's rich and powerful, and goblins are recognized as people. Vimes returns to the city with his family, his holiday having gone exactly as everyone expected.

recaps.text: Previously, in earlier books: Sam Vimes rose from a drunken night watchman to Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch, rebuilding it into a large mixed force of humans, dwarfs, trolls, werewolves, and others, and became Duke of Ankh through his marriage to the aristocratic Lady Sybil Ramkin, a title he has never enjoyed. He answers, grudgingly, to Lord Vetinari, the Patrician, who finds him useful precisely because he cannot be bought or flattered. Vimes distrusts privilege, especially his own, polices by the principle that the law applies to everybody or it is not the law, and keeps a tight hold on his own temper because he knows what is underneath it. During an earlier case an ancient dwarfish thing got into his head and has remained there since, watching, as a kind of unwelcome guardian. He and Sybil have a young son, and Vimes's fiercest personal rule is that he is home to read to the boy at six o'clock.

Vimes is manoeuvred by his wife, with Lord Vetinari's approval, into taking the first holiday of his adult life: a stay at the Ramkin family's country estate, along with Lady Sybil, six-year-old Young Sam, and Willikins. The countryside receives him as a duke, which he loathes, and he discovers immediately that he does not know how to stop being a policeman. He notices the things the locals no longer see: the careful way people talk around certain subjects, the deference that goes slightly wrong, and the goblins who live in the hills above the estate and are regarded by everybody as vermin, which under the law here is exactly what they are.

Vimes explores the village and its pub, where the landlord recognizes him faster than any country publican should. He meets the local gentry at dinner and finds them polite, incurious, and united in the view that goblins are pests to be cleared. Young Sam, meanwhile, has fallen in love with a local children's author's book about animal droppings and pursues the subject relentlessly. Vimes takes note of a young local man who talks to him about the goblins and then is not seen again, and of the fact that nobody appears to consider this worth reporting. The country grows quietly more hostile the longer he asks questions, and the smell of a crime he cannot yet name settles over the whole estate.

Vimes finds the body of a young goblin woman who has been beaten to death. Under local law this is not murder, because a goblin is not a person, and the district has no intention of treating it as one. Feeney Upshot, the young and entirely untrained chief constable, arrives and arrests Vimes for the killing; Vimes, who could have stopped him, allows it, then takes charge of both the arrest and the constable, and begins turning him into a real policeman. Back in Ankh-Morpork the Watch has picked up a goblin item as evidence, and Sergeant Colon, who has handled it, is being slowly and frighteningly taken over by whatever is bound up in it. Vimes starts building a case in a place where the local magistrates, the local money, and the local law are all on the other side.

Vimes goes up into the goblin caves and learns what the district has been careful not to know: the goblins have a religion, a language, a craft, and a rigorous moral code, and one young goblin woman, taught by the local children's author, plays the harp well enough to settle the question of what goblins are for anyone honest enough to listen. The reason for the murder becomes clear as the trade behind it surfaces: goblins have been rounded up and shipped abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations, with smuggled goods carried on the return trips, organized and financed by people with land, titles, and friends. Enforcing it is Stratford, a local killer who works without hesitation or feeling, and who now knows that the Duke of Ankh is asking questions.

With Feeney beside him and a goblin guide who knows every inch of the country, Vimes goes after the boats carrying the captured goblins downriver. A storm turns into a flood, and the pursuit becomes a night run down a rising river that no sane person would attempt, ending with Vimes half drowned and washed up a long way from anywhere. In the city, Wee Mad Arthur works the docks and the warehouses from angles nobody thinks to guard, following the smuggled goods back to the people paying for them, and turns up an unexpected fact about his own origins along the way. Vimes survives, catches up with the boats, and takes them, and the surviving goblins are freed and, for the first time, in the hands of somebody prepared to treat what was done to them as a crime.

The pursuit ends downriver at Quirm, where Vimes, filthy and exhausted, hands over prisoners, evidence, and a case, and is put back together by the local Watch and eventually by his wife. Stratford, however, is not among those taken, and is loose and moving. Vimes returns to the estate and then to Ankh-Morpork with everything he needs: witnesses, documents, the boats, and the survivors. Sergeant Colon is freed of what he was carrying once the goblin property is returned to the people it belongs to. Feeney, having done everything asked of him and rather more, is no longer a village constable in anything but title, and the question is no longer whether the crime can be proved but whether a court will accept that a crime against goblins is a crime at all.

The case moves to the city, where the law, not the arrests, is the real battleground: everything Vimes has depends on goblins being people, and at present they legally are not. Vetinari, who has been several steps ahead throughout, arranges the occasion for settling it, a concert at the Opera House before an audience of the city's wealthiest and most influential. Vimes prepares the evidence, Miss Beedle prepares her pupil, and the aristocratic families behind the trade prepare to brazen it out. Stratford, who has nothing left to lose, makes his own preparations, and they involve Vimes's household.

At the Opera House, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp in front of the city's rich and powerful, and an audience raised to believe goblins were vermin listens to one make music. That, together with the case Vimes has built, is enough: the law is changed and goblins become people, with everything that follows from it. Stratford makes his last attempt, going after Vimes and his family, and is taken; the estate is set alight in the course of it. The aristocrat who financed the slaving trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that strip him of everything, the freed goblins are given standing and protection, Sergeant Colon recovers, and Feeney Upshot ends the affair as a genuine policeman with a career in front of him. Vimes goes home to Ankh-Morpork with his wife and son, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, exactly as everyone expected, into police work.
